chapters.title: Chapter 5: Tax, Tracking, and Your Deal Checklist

lessons.title: Tracking Deal Announcements on BSE, NSE, and screener.in

children.text: Everything you have learned in this course lives in documents that are free, public and usually online within minutes of a board meeting ending. Yet most retail investors learn about deals from a television ticker, a WhatsApp forward or a headline written by someone who has not read the scheme either. The gap between the two is where mistakes happen. This lesson shows you exactly where each document sits, what it tells you, and how to keep track of a deal from announcement to completion without paying for anything.

body.text: Every number that matters in a deal, the ratio, the price, the record date, the conditions, comes from a primary document filed with BSE and NSE. News reports summarise those documents, often selectively. Train yourself to go to the filing first and the headline second.

body.label: BSE Corporate Announcements
body.description: Filter by company, date and category to read board outcomes, schemes, record date notices and cost apportionment filings at the source.

body.label: NSE India
body.description: Search a company and open its corporate filings for announcements, board meetings, corporate actions and scheme documents.

body.label: Screener.in
body.description: The fastest single page for a company: announcements, quarterly results, shareholding pattern, ROCE and borrowings, all in one place.

body.text: Screener.in is the best starting point and the exchanges are the best finishing point. Use screener.in to spot that something happened and to check the numbers around it, then open the actual filing on BSE or NSE before you act on it.

children.text: The Rules That Force Companies to Tell You

Disclosure is not a courtesy. SEBI's Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements Regulations set out what must be filed and when. Material events, including deal approvals, must be disclosed promptly. Draft schemes go to the exchanges under Regulation 37 before the company can approach the NCLT. Record dates must be notified in advance. Separately, under the Takeover Regulations you met in Lesson 2.3, anyone crossing 5% of a listed company must disclose it, and further changes of 2% must also be disclosed.

stats.label: Draft scheme filing

body.title: How much room is left?
body.prompt: On 1 April, the promoter group of a listed company held 58% and has bought shares during the year to reach 61.5%. Ignoring any open offer, how many more percentage points can it acquire this financial year before crossing the creeping acquisition limit?
body.explanation: The creeping limit allows up to 5% in a financial year for holders between 25% and 75%. The promoters have used 61.5% minus 58% = 3.5%, leaving 1.5 percentage points. Buying more would trigger an open offer. Quarterly shareholding patterns and Takeover Code disclosures let you watch this build up.

children.text: A Research Routine That Takes Fifteen Minutes

body.title: What to check at each stage of a deal

events.title: Read the board outcome and press release
events.description: Note the deal type, ratio or price, stated motives and whether the counterparty is a related party. Check the stock's reaction on both the acquirer and the target.

events.title: Open the scheme, valuation report and fairness opinion
events.description: Check the appointed date, what assets and liabilities move, cross-holdings, and how the ratio was derived, using Lesson 2.2.

events.title: Track approvals
events.description: Watch for the observation letter, CCI or RBI approvals, and any regulator queries. Filings appear on the exchanges as they happen.

events.title: Read the notice and vote
events.description: The notice carries the independent directors' report and explains whether the public shareholder majority condition applies.

events.title: Watch for the record date
events.description: Then note the special session price, the credit of new shares and the listing date.

events.title: Collect the cost apportionment announcement
events.description: File it with your tax papers, as Lesson 4.3 and Lesson 5.1 explained.

body.title: Which document answers the question?
body.question: You want to know why the swap ratio in a pending merger gives the target's shareholders less than the target's market price suggests. Which document should you open first?
options: The valuation report filed with the scheme, which shows the methods, values per share and weights used
body.explanation: The valuation report is the only document that shows how the ratio was built, including the weight given to market price, DCF and net asset value. The fairness opinion and independent directors' report sit alongside it and explain why the board considers the ratio fair.

columns.label: Primary: exchange filings
points: Complete, signed and legally binding on the company
Contains ratios, dates, conditions and the fine print
Available free to everyone at the same time
Longer to read, with legal language
The only version that matters if you need to act

columns.label: Secondary: news, videos and social media
points: Often omits conditions, timelines and approval risk
Headline numbers can mix enterprise value and equity value
Anonymous tips and target prices are unverifiable
Useful to learn that something happened, not to decide what to do

body.title: How to read a 150-page scheme in twenty minutes

children.text: You do not need to read a scheme cover to cover. Go straight to these clauses, which usually appear in this order.
Definitions: appointed date, effective date and what counts as the undertaking being transferred.
Share entitlement or consideration clause: the ratio, in words and figures, plus the treatment of fractional entitlements.
Cancellation of cross-holdings: whether shares held between the companies are extinguished, which changes post-deal ownership.
Accounting treatment: how the transaction will be recorded, including goodwill or reserves adjustments.
Conditions precedent and the clause allowing withdrawal: what must happen for the scheme to take effect, and who can walk away.
Debt and employee transfer clauses: which company carries the borrowings and where employees land, which matters for a demerger.

body.title: The filing that starts it all
body.textWithBlank: A listed company must file its draft scheme of arrangement with the stock exchanges under Regulation ___ of SEBI's LODR Regulations before approaching the NCLT.
body.explanation: Regulation 37 filings are public, so you can read the scheme, valuation report and fairness opinion on the BSE or NSE website months before you vote.

body.title: The WhatsApp tip
body.scenario: A group message says: "Confirmed: Vindhya Industries demerging its chemicals arm next week, ratio 1:1, stock will double. Buy before announcement." You own some Vindhya shares. The stock is up 7% today with no news you can see.
body.prompt: How would you verify this, and what would you do?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Check the exchanges first. Open BSE and NSE announcements for Vindhya. A genuine scheme would appear as a board outcome, and a board meeting would have been notified in advance.
2. Look for a clarification filing. When a stock moves on rumours, exchanges often seek a clarification, and the company's reply is filed publicly.
3. Check the shareholding pattern and any recent Takeover Code disclosures for unusual buying.
4. Treat the message as unverified. Acting on unpublished price-sensitive information, if it were genuine, is illegal insider trading. If it is not genuine, it is simply someone talking up a position.
5. If the demerger is later announced, nothing is lost: as Chapter 4 showed, receiving demerger shares does not create value by itself, and you will have months to assess the scheme before the record date.
6. Do not buy on a forward. If you want more Vindhya, base it on the business, not on a rumoured ratio that a stranger has invented.

body.text: Trading on unpublished price-sensitive information received from an insider is a serious offence under SEBI's insider trading regulations, and the penalties fall on the person who trades, not on whoever forwarded the message. If a tip is genuinely non-public, that is a reason to stay away, not a reason to act.

body.title: Your deal tracking routine
steps: Bookmark the BSE announcements page and the screener.in pages of stocks you own
Check announcements for your holdings once a week, and after any unexplained price move
When a deal is announced, download the board outcome, scheme, valuation report and fairness opinion the same week
Keep a simple file per deal with the ratio, key dates and pending approvals
Diarise the shareholder vote, record date and listing date
Save the cost apportionment announcement with your tax records
Compare promised synergies with what management reports a year later

cards.definition: The first filing after a board approves a deal, carrying the ratio and rationale.
The draft scheme, valuation report and fairness opinion filed with the exchanges before the NCLT.
The exchanges' response after SEBI's comments, needed before approaching the NCLT.
The detailed document for an open offer or delisting, carrying price, size, dates and the tendering process.
A filing when someone crosses 5% of a listed company, and on every 2% change after that.
The company's filing telling shareholders how to split cost between parent and resulting company after a demerger.
A company's public reply when an exchange asks about a market rumour.

points: Every deal number you need is in a free public filing on BSE or NSE, usually the same day the board meets.
Use screener.in to spot activity and check the numbers, then read the actual filing before acting.
The scheme, valuation report and fairness opinion are filed together under Regulation 37, long before you vote.
Watch shareholding patterns, Takeover Code disclosures and bulk deals for signs of activity before any announcement.
A promoter between 25% and 75% can add only 5% in a financial year, so creeping purchases are visible and countable.
Ignore tips. If information is genuinely unpublished and price-sensitive, trading on it is illegal.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment, tax or legal advice. Vindhya Industries is fictional. Regulatory references are simplified summaries of SEBI's LODR and Takeover Regulations as generally applied, and website layouts and disclosure requirements change over time. Always check the current filing requirements and the exchange websites directly.
